error_modes.label: Release of crosswind controls, crab and runway alignment on the takeoff leg

texts.0: SP carried the takeoff roll control inputs into the air and did not release the crosswind controls after becoming airborne, so the aircraft was not allowed to crab into the wind. The upwind wing dipped towards the ground, the climb was flown uncoordinated and the aircraft drifted downwind with a track error of more than 10 degrees from the runway alignment on the takeoff leg. IP took the controls, levelled the wings, established the crab and restored the runway alignment.
texts.1: SP, due to the into-wind aileron being held as a habit from the takeoff roll, did not release the crosswind controls after lift off and did not adjust the rudder as the wheels left the ground and airspeed increased. The wing stayed low, the ball was out of centre and the deviation from runway alignment reached the 10 degree limit before IP prompted verbally to release the controls and crab into the wind. SP then established a coordinated crabbed climb.
texts.2: SP released the crosswind controls late after becoming airborne and made the rudder adjustment only after the drift became visible, so the crab was established behind the aircraft. Track error passed 5 degrees and reached about 8 degrees from the runway alignment before SP recognized the drift, levelled the wings and crabbed into the wind. Coordination was restored by SP without intervention.
texts.3: SP released the crosswind controls after takeoff and allowed the aircraft to crab into the wind, adjusting the rudder as the wheels left the ground and airspeed increased. The climb was flown in coordinated flight and runway alignment on the takeoff leg was maintained within 5 degrees. The upwind wing was never allowed to dip towards the ground.
texts.4: SP transitioned from crosswind takeoff controls to a coordinated crabbed climb with no perceptible wing drop and no yaw excursion as the wheels left the ground. Runway alignment on the takeoff leg was held with negligible drift and the ball stayed centred throughout the climb. The crosswind was compensated as a matter of technique rather than by correction.
texts.marginal: SP maintained runway alignment on the takeoff leg within standards, but the alignment was held by repeated corrections and a small amount of into-wind aileron was still carried into the climb. The deviations stayed inside the tolerance, yet the drift downwind reappeared each time attention moved to the cleanup. SP is expected to release the crosswind controls fully after takeoff and to hold a single stable crab angle in coordinated flight.

texts_at.0: SP released the crosswind controls and established the crab into the wind with the IP calling for the rudder adjustment as the wheels left the ground, due to first exposure to releasing a crosswind correction at the same instant the aircraft becomes airborne. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to release the crosswind controls and crab into the wind independently on the next crosswind takeoff, without the rudder adjustment being called.
texts_at.1: SP released the crosswind controls and established a crab into the wind to the level expected at this stage, with the runway alignment error on the takeoff leg reaching about 10 degrees, near the upper part of the tolerance, due to the into-wind aileron being held as a habit from the takeoff roll into the initial climb. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to release the into-wind aileron the instant the wheels leave the ground, not carry it as a habit into the climb.
texts_at.2: SP levelled the wings, established the crab and restored the runway alignment, correcting a deviation of about 7 degrees, due to the crosswind controls being released late after becoming airborne and the rudder adjustment made only once the drift had become visible. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to adjust the rudder at the same instant the crosswind controls are released, not after the drift is seen.
texts_at.3: SP released the crosswind controls after takeoff and allowed the aircraft to crab into the wind, adjusting the rudder as the wheels left the ground, with runway alignment held to about 4 degrees, due to the release itself being made a beat later than the exact instant of lift-off. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to release the crosswind controls at the exact instant the wheels leave the ground.

texts_above.1: SP released the crosswind controls, with the runway alignment error on the takeoff leg reaching about 8 degrees before the wings were levelled and the crab established. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the crosswind controls had been released late after becoming airborne, levelled the wings, established the crab and restored the runway alignment with the deviation held to about 7 degrees, with no intervention. Adjusting the rudder at the same instant the crosswind controls are released, rather than after the drift is seen, would remove the correction from the climb. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent crosswind-release technique.
texts_above.3: SP released the crosswind controls after takeoff and allowed the aircraft to crab into the wind, adjusting the rudder as the wheels left the ground and airspeed increased, the climb flown in coordinated flight with runway alignment held within about 3 degrees. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined crosswind-release technique.
texts_above.4: SP transitioned from crosswind takeoff controls to a coordinated crabbed climb with no perceptible wing drop and no yaw excursion as the wheels left the ground, runway alignment held to about a degree and the ball centred throughout the climb. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to faultless crosswind-release technique.

error_modes.label: Use of outside references for pitch, heading and bank, crosschecked with the instruments

texts.0: SP made all pitch and bank changes on the attitude indicator with a usable horizon and outside references available, and did not use section lines, a prominent point near the horizon or other outside references for heading. The scan stayed inside the cockpit, each indication was chased in turn and the departure profile diverged by more than 300 feet in altitude and more than 10 degrees in heading, with no lookout maintained during the transition. IP took the controls, directed the scan outside and re-established the profile.
texts.1: SP, having reverted to an instrument scan during the transition to the flight areas, did not select an outside reference near the horizon for heading and did not fly the climb attitude against the horizon. The corrections lagged the indications and the deviations reached the 300 feet and 10 degree limits before IP prompted verbally to look outside and to use the instruments only as a crosscheck. SP then flew the remainder of the departure on outside references.
texts.2: SP established the climb on outside references but returned to the attitude indicator for each correction, so the pitch changes became small chased inputs rather than a single attitude adjustment. Altitude drifted about 200 feet and heading some 7 degrees before SP recognized the closed scan, moved the reference outside and stabilized the climb. The correction was made in good time without intervention.
texts.3: SP made pitch and bank changes using outside references and crosschecked heading on the EHSI and wings level on the attitude indicator, rather than flying the instruments directly. The departure profile was held within 150 feet and 5 degrees while the lookout was maintained. The instruments confirmed the picture instead of driving it.
texts.4: SP flew the departure climb primarily on outside references, selecting a prominent point near the horizon for heading and holding the climb attitude against the horizon, with the EHSI and attitude indicator used only as periodic confirmation. Altitude and heading deviations were negligible and the lookout was continuous. The balance between outside references and instruments was exactly as the technique describes.
texts.marginal: SP held the departure profile within standards, but the corrections were initiated from the instruments and the outside references were used mainly to confirm what had already been read inside. The deviations remained inside the tolerance, yet the scan spends more time in the cockpit than the visual departure requires. SP is expected to fly pitch, bank and heading on outside references when they are available and to crosscheck the EHSI and attitude indicator rather than lead with them.

texts_at.0: SP flew the departure climb on outside references with the IP calling attention back outside each time the scan settled on the attitude indicator, due to first exposure to leading a correction from outside references rather than from the instrument. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to fly the departure climb on outside references independently on the next sortie, without attention being called back outside.
texts_at.1: SP flew the departure climb primarily on outside references to the level expected at this stage, with altitude reaching about 300 feet and heading about 10 degrees off, near the upper part of both tolerances, due to the scan returning to the attitude indicator for each correction rather than staying on the outside picture through it. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to keep the correction itself on the outside reference, using the instruments only to confirm it afterward.
texts_at.2: SP moved the reference outside and stabilized the climb without intervention, correcting altitude of about 200 feet and heading of about 7 degrees, due to the climb being established on outside references but the scan then returning to the attitude indicator for each correction. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to hold the outside reference through the correction itself, not only through the initial attitude setting.
texts_at.3: SP made pitch and bank changes using outside references and crosschecked heading on the EHSI and wings level on the attitude indicator, holding altitude to about 110 feet and heading to about 4 degrees, due to one crosscheck of the EHSI being made a beat before the outside picture confirmed the same heading. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to let the outside picture lead every crosscheck rather than the instrument.

texts_above.1: SP flew the departure climb on outside references, with altitude reaching about 270 feet and heading about 8 degrees off before the scan was moved back outside and the climb stabilized. The correction followed a verbal call from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP recognized the scan had returned to the attitude indicator for each correction instead of staying on the outside picture, moved the reference back outside and stabilized the climb with altitude held to about 200 feet and heading to about 7 degrees, without intervention. Holding the outside reference through the correction itself, rather than only through the initial attitude setting, would remove the correction from the climb. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good outside-reference technique.
texts_above.3: SP made pitch and bank changes using outside references and crosschecked heading on the EHSI and wings level on the attitude indicator rather than flying the instruments directly, the departure profile held within about 110 feet and 4 degrees while the lookout was maintained. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good crosscheck discipline.
texts_above.4: SP flew the departure climb primarily on outside references, selecting a prominent point near the horizon for heading and holding the climb attitude against the horizon, altitude and heading deviations of a few tens of feet and about a degree with continuous lookout. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent crosscheck discipline.

error_modes.label: Climb check passing 10.000 feet MSL and operations check at initial level off

texts.0: SP did not initiate the climb check passing 10.000 feet MSL and did not carry out the operations check at initial level off, so neither the climb nor the level off was supported by the required checks. When the omission was raised, both checks were started together at the top of the climb while the aircraft was left unattended in pitch and power and the assigned altitude was exceeded by more than 300 feet. IP took the controls, recovered the altitude and directed the checks to be completed in the correct order.
texts.1: SP, due to the checks being treated as time permitting items rather than as fixed points in the departure, passed 10.000 feet MSL without initiating the climb check and reached the assigned altitude without an operations check. Attention shifted to the checks after the level off and the altitude deviation reached the 300 feet limit before IP prompted verbally to fly the aircraft first and then complete the checks. SP then stabilized the aircraft and completed both checks.
texts.2: SP initiated the climb check several thousand feet after passing 10.000 feet MSL and started the operations check before the aircraft was stabilized on the assigned altitude. Altitude drifted about 200 feet during the check before SP recognized the priority, returned to aircraft control and then finished the check. The recovery was made by SP without intervention.
texts.3: SP initiated the climb check passing 10.000 feet MSL and conducted the operations check at initial level off, interleaving both with aircraft control so that the assigned altitude was held within 150 feet. Each item was read and acted on rather than recited. Neither check displaced the flying task.
texts.4: SP initiated the climb check exactly passing 10.000 feet MSL and completed the operations check once stabilized at initial level off, with negligible altitude and airspeed variation during either check. The checks were integrated with the cross-check and the lookout so that nothing was interrupted. Timing and execution were as required by the flight manual.
texts.marginal: SP completed the climb check and the operations check within standards, but both were started slightly late and were run as a rapid recitation while the aircraft was still being stabilized. The parameters stayed inside the tolerance, yet the checks are still fitted around the flying rather than anticipated at their trigger points. SP is expected to anticipate 10.000 feet MSL and the initial level off as fixed triggers and to complete each check with the aircraft trimmed and stable.

texts_at.0: SP initiated the climb check and the operations check with the IP calling the trigger points of ten thousand feet MSL and the initial level off, due to first exposure to anticipating two fixed trigger points rather than fitting the checks around the flying task. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to initiate both checks independently at their trigger points on the next sortie, without the points being called.
texts_at.1: SP initiated the climb check passing ten thousand feet MSL and conducted the operations check at initial level off to the level expected at this stage, with altitude reaching about 300 feet during the check, near the upper part of the tolerance, due to the operations check being started a moment before the aircraft was fully stabilized on the assigned altitude. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to confirm the aircraft is stabilized on altitude before the operations check is started, not while it is still settling.
texts_at.2: SP returned to aircraft control and then finished the check, correcting a deviation of about 200 feet, due to the operations check being started before the aircraft was stabilized on the assigned altitude, which let attention shift away from the flying task during the check. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to prioritize stabilizing on altitude over starting the check by even a few seconds.
texts_at.3: SP initiated the climb check passing ten thousand feet MSL and conducted the operations check at initial level off, interleaving both with aircraft control so the assigned altitude was held within about 150 feet, due to the operations check beginning a beat before the level off was fully settled rather than immediately after. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to confirm the level off is fully settled before starting the operations check.

texts_above.1: SP initiated the climb check and the operations check, with altitude reaching about 270 feet during the check, near the upper part of the tolerance, before aircraft control was reclaimed and the checks were completed. The return to aircraft control followed a verbal call from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP recognized that the operations check had been started before the aircraft was stabilized on the assigned altitude, returned to aircraft control first and then finished the check with the deviation held to about 200 feet, without intervention. Confirming the aircraft is stabilized on altitude before the operations check is started, rather than while it is still settling, would remove the correction from the sequence. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound check-timing discipline.
texts_above.3: SP initiated the climb check passing ten thousand feet MSL and conducted the operations check at initial level off, interleaving both with aircraft control so that the assigned altitude was held within about 110 feet, with each item read and acted on rather than recited. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed check-timing technique.
texts_above.4: SP initiated the climb check exactly passing ten thousand feet MSL and completed the operations check once stabilized at initial level off, altitude and airspeed variation of only a few tens of feet during either check, both integrated with the cross-check and the lookout so nothing was interrupted. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional check-timing technique.
